c.tagline: Where granite peaks vanish into seas of cloud and Ming-dynasty villages sleep in the valleys below.

card: Credit cards are rarely accepted outside international hotels; WeChat Pay and Alipay are used for almost everything — set up mobile payment before arrival and carry some cash as backup

taxi.fareNote: Insist on the meter; airport and Tangkou (mountain base) drivers often push flat 'special' fares — agree a price upfront if they refuse to use it

emergency.medical: 120 (ambulance); Huangshan Second People's Hospital in Tunxi
emergency.note: Mountain rescue teams patrol Huangshan's main trails; English is rare on emergency lines — have a Mandarin speaker or your hotel call for you

walk: Tunxi's Old Street and riverside areas are very walkable; the mountain itself demands serious hiking or cable cars, and the ancient villages are best explored on foot along cobblestone lanes

safety.safety: Very safe for solo travelers, including women; petty crime is rare
safety.crime: Low — occasional overcharging by unlicensed taxis or tour touts near the mountain entrance is the main annoyance

hood_landmark.Tunxi Old Street: Zhen Hai Bridge and the Ming-Qing shopping street
hood_landmark.Huangshan Scenic Area: Mount Huangshan's granite peaks and Sea of Clouds
hood_landmark.Hongcun & Xidi Ancient Villages: Hongcun's Moon Pond and South Lake

avoid.reason: Watch for touts and inflated tea/souvenir prices around Tunxi Old Street and cable-car queue jumping in peak season.

hood_desc: A pedestrian Ming-and-Qing-dynasty street of black-tile, white-wall shophouses selling Huizhou ink, tea, and carved inkstones — the city's most walkable, central base.
The granite spine of Mount Huangshan itself — pine-clad peaks, cloud seas, and sunrise views reached by cable car or a punishing stone-step climb from Tangkou village.
Twin UNESCO-listed Huizhou villages of whitewashed courtyard homes reflected in ox-shaped ponds, a short bus ride from Tunxi.
The old Huizhou prefectural capital, its stone memorial archways and Doushan Street preserving 500 years of merchant-clan history.
A quieter Taoist sacred mountain south of the city, its cliffside temples and grottoes drawing far fewer crowds than Huangshan itself.

water.note: Drink bottled or boiled water only, as everywhere in mainland China.

transit.sys: City buses (Huangshan Bus Group) plus scenic-area shuttle buses
transit.pay: Cash or QR code (WeChat/Alipay) on buses; no unified transit card for tourists
transit.map: Routes aren't on Google/Apple Maps — use Baidu Maps or Amap (Gaode)
transit.note: Most sights outside Tunxi require taxis, Didi, or tour buses; there is no rail/metro system in the city

transport.air: Huangshan Tunxi International Airport (TXN), ~7 km from Tunxi, with flights to Shanghai, Beijing, Guangzhou, and other major Chinese cities
transport.train: Huangshan North railway station sits on the Hefei–Fuzhou and Shanghai–Kunming high-speed lines — about 3 hrs from Shanghai, 1.5 hrs from Hangzhou
transport.bus: Long-distance buses connect Huangshan to Hangzhou, Shanghai, and Nanjing; local buses run from Tunxi to Tangkou (mountain base) and the ancient villages
transport.ferry: None — Huangshan is inland with no scheduled passenger ferry service
transport.car: Self-driving or a hired car is common for reaching Hongcun, Xidi, and Shexian; roads are good but mountain-area driving and parking get congested in peak season

airport.name: Huangshan Tunxi International Airport
airport.transport: Taxi ~$8-10 metered fare into town; airport shuttle bus to central Tunxi also available

net.m: Good 4G/5G coverage in Tunxi and along main roads; patchy on remote mountain trails
net.w: Free wifi in most hotels and cafes, though speeds vary
net.ops: China Mobile, China Unicom, China Telecom
net.gb: ~$3-5 per GB on a prepaid tourist SIM
net.fwn: The Great Firewall blocks Google, WhatsApp, Instagram, and Facebook — install a VPN before arrival
net.ap: Buy a SIM or eSIM at Shanghai/Hangzhou airport before onward travel; Tunxi Airport's counter has limited stock

tip.s: Not expected — tipping isn't part of Chinese service culture and can even confuse staff
tip.r: No tipping at restaurants; a service charge is occasionally added automatically at upscale hotel restaurants

food.name: Chou guiyu (stinky mandarin fish)
food.desc: Mandarin fish lightly fermented in salted barrels then pan-fried and braised with pork and chilli; pungent on the nose, sweet and firm on the fork.

places.name: Laoma Restaurant
places.note: Home-style Huizhou kitchen whose braised stinky mandarin fish is its signature.

places.name: Laojie Diyi Lou
places.area: Tunxi Old Street, near the memorial archway
places.note: The best-reviewed dining room on Old Street; big portions, fast service, fair prices.

places.name: Dasha Huicai Garden
places.note: Huizhou specialist that pairs the fish with hairy tofu as a set.

food.name: Huizhou braised pork
food.desc: Pork belly red-braised slowly with rock sugar, soy and rice wine until glossy, often layered with preserved mustard greens.

places.name: Laojie Diyi Lou
places.note: Full sweep of the Huizhou repertoire in one menu, easiest first meal in town.

places.name: Huashan Huiyan Huifu Cuisine
places.note: Hotel restaurant doing polished versions of the regional classics.

places.name: Laoma Restaurant
places.note: Unfussy local favourite, strongest on slow-braised meat dishes.

food.name: Mao doufu (hairy tofu)
food.desc: Tofu grown with a white fuzz of edible mould, pan-fried until crisp and eaten with chilli sauce; a Huizhou street-food rite of passage.

places.name: Tunxi Old Street stalls
places.note: Griddle carts along the flagstones fry it to order all afternoon and evening.

places.name: Laojie Diyi Lou
places.note: Sit-down version if you would rather try it with a full meal.

places.name: Liyang In Xiang lanes
places.note: Restored lane district with food stalls and bars, quieter than Old Street.

food.name: Huangshan shaobing
food.desc: Crisp sesame-crusted pastry stuffed with dried mustard greens and pork fat, baked against the wall of a clay oven; also called meigancai shaobing.

places.name: Tunxi Old Street bakeries
places.note: Several clay-oven counters sell them hot by the bagful; buy where the queue is.

places.name: Liyang In Xiang lanes
places.note: Evening stalls bake them fresh alongside local snacks and tea.

places.name: Tangkou town food street
places.note: The standard breakfast bought before the cable car up the mountain.

food.name: Hu Shi yi pin guo
food.desc: Layered one-pot casserole of bamboo shoots, tofu skin, meatballs, pork and egg dumplings simmered together; the classic Huizhou winter feast dish.

places.name: Laoma Restaurant
places.note: Traditional preparation in a clay pot, best ordered for a group.

places.name: Laojie Diyi Lou
places.note: Also does a well-known braised chicken in a pot on the same menu.

places.name: Huashan Huiyan Huifu Cuisine
places.note: Comfortable option with English-friendly picture menus.

food.name: Wenzheng bamboo shoots with ham
food.desc: Spring bamboo shoots from the hills braised with cured Huizhou ham; a delicate, salty-sweet dish that defines the region's mountain cooking.

places.name: Laojie Diyi Lou
places.note: Seasonal mountain vegetables and fungus dishes are a strength here.

places.name: Dasha Huicai Garden
places.note: Specialist Huizhou kitchen with the wild-shoot and fungus classics.

places.name: Laoma Restaurant
places.note: Cooks it as a home dish, less oily than the banquet version.

food.name: Huangshan Maofeng tea
food.desc: One of China's ten famous teas, a delicate green picked on the Yellow Mountain slopes in early spring and brewed pale and orchid-scented.

places.name: Xie Yuda Tea House
places.note: House founded in 1875 that made Maofeng famous; tastings and shop on Old Street.

places.name: Tunxi Old Street tea shops
places.note: Dozens of merchants will brew before you buy; ask for the current spring picking.

places.name: Liyang In Xiang teahouses
places.note: Riverside teahouses for a slower sit-down pot away from the crowds.

food.name: Huizhou rice wine
food.desc: Cloudy, gently sweet fermented rice wine served warm in small bowls with heavy braised dishes; low in alcohol and made locally.

places.name: Laoma Restaurant
places.note: House jugs poured alongside the stinky fish, the traditional pairing.

places.name: Laojie Diyi Lou
places.note: Carries local rice wine and Anhui grain spirits by the bottle.

places.name: Liyang In Xiang lanes
places.note: Small bars in the restored lanes serve it warm on cold nights.

landmarks: Huangshan (Yellow Mountain) Scenic Area
China's most painted mountain, a UNESCO landscape of granite spires, gnarled pines and swirling seas of cloud that inspired centuries of poets.
Hongcun Ancient Village
A UNESCO-listed Ming-era water village whose moon pond and whitewashed Huizhou mansions starred in Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon.
Xidi Ancient Village
Hongcun's UNESCO twin, an exquisitely preserved merchant village of carved stone archways, black-tiled roofs and nearly a thousand years of Huizhou heritage.
West Sea Grand Canyon (Xihai Great Canyon)
Yellow Mountain's most thrilling sector, where plank paths and stairways cling to sheer granite walls above a fantasy landscape of mist-wrapped pinnacles.
Greeting-Guests Pine (Yingkesong)
An 800-year-old pine extending a welcoming bough beside Jade Screen Peak, so iconic it appears in the Great Hall of the People.
Tunxi Old Street (Tunxi Laojie)
A flagstone street of Ming and Qing storefronts in Huangshan city, perfect for browsing ink stones, tea and street snacks beneath red lanterns.
Bright Summit (Guangming Peak)
Yellow Mountain's second-highest point and its finest sunrise stage, where crowds gather at dawn to watch clouds ignite over an ocean of peaks.
Tangyue Memorial Archways
Seven monumental stone arches marching across the fields near Shexian, Ming and Qing tributes to the loyalty and virtue of the Bao family.
Huizhou Ancient City (Shexian)
One of China's four great ancient cities, a walled county seat of gate towers, the grand Xuguo Stone Archway and living Huizhou traditions.
Chengkan Village
A feng-shui masterpiece village laid out on the bagua pattern, its Baolun Hall ranking among the finest Ming ancestral buildings in southern China.

train.note: Huangshan has no international trains. Huangshan North, open since 2015, is the high-speed station with services to Hangzhou in about 1.5 hours plus Shanghai, Nanjing, Nanchang, Qingdao, Fuzhou, Guangzhou and Beijing; the older Huangshan station in Tunxi handles conventional trains, including an overnight service from Shanghai via Suzhou and Nanjing that takes about 11 hours and arrives around 07:00, leaving you a full day on the mountain. Book on 12306 with your passport, and remember that both stations are in Huangshan City (Tunxi), an hour short of the mountain itself.

bus.note: No international coaches serve Huangshan. Direct buses run from Shanghai and Hangzhou to the main Huangshan (Tunxi) bus station, and from there frequent services continue to Tangkou at the foot of the mountain in about an hour, with some long-distance coaches running through to Tangkou directly. Return coaches from the mountain generally leave in the early to mid afternoon, so do not leave the descent too late. Tickets are sold at the terminal counters.

ferry.note: There are no passenger ferry services to or from Huangshan; it is an inland city in the hills of southern Anhui. The only boats in the area are sightseeing cruises on Taiping Lake, on the northern side of the mountain, which are sold as an excursion rather than as transport.

half.name: Wuyuan Ancient Villages
half.blurb: A cluster of Hui-style villages with white-walled courtyard houses, said to be among the best-preserved in China, roughly two hours from Huangshan by road.

half.name: Mount Qiyun (Qiyunshan)
half.blurb: A Taoist mountain in Xiuning County dotted with cliffside temples, grottoes, and carved inscriptions, reached in under two hours from central Huangshan.

half.name: Jingdezhen
half.blurb: China's historic porcelain-making city, with kiln museums and working ceramic workshops, roughly two hours away by train.

half.name: Qimen
half.blurb: A tea-growing county southwest of Huangshan known for Keemun black tea plantations and processing workshops.
